measures.title: Public Question #1: Bail (Article 1, Section 17)
measures.summary: This constitutional amendment would let courts deny bail to a person charged with an offense other than murder or treason if the proof is evident or the presumption strong, and the state proves by clear and convincing evidence that no release conditions will reasonably protect the safety of any other person or the community.
measures.forMeans: A yes vote amends the constitution so courts can deny bail in more cases, beyond murder and treason, when both conditions are met.
measures.againstMeans: A no vote keeps the current rule, under which bail may be denied only for murder or treason when the proof is evident or the presumption strong.

measures.title: Public Question #2: Residency of City and Town Court Judges (Article 6, Section 6)
measures.summary: This constitutional amendment would let a city or town court judge live in the county where the court is located, or in the bordering county closest to the city or town, instead of having to live in the city or town itself.
measures.forMeans: A yes vote amends the constitution so city and town court judges may live in the court's county or in the nearest bordering county.
measures.againstMeans: A no vote keeps the current requirement that city and town court judges live in the city or town where they serve.

18.measuresNote: Both statewide questions are constitutional amendments referred by the legislature, and the full ballot text is in the WFYI voter guide and on your county's sample ballot.

measures.title: Amendment 3 (Legislatively referred constitutional amendment, HCS HJR 73)
measures.summary: Would repeal the reproductive healthcare rights amendment voters approved in 2024 (Article I, Section 36). It would allow abortion only in medical emergencies, for fetal anomalies, and for rape or incest before 12 weeks, and would allow laws regulating abortion. It would require parental or judicial consent for minors and prohibit gender transition procedures for minors.
measures.forMeans: A yes vote repeals Article I, Section 36. It allows abortion to be restricted to medical emergencies, fetal anomalies, and rape or incest under 12 weeks. It allows abortion regulation, requires informed consent (including parental or judicial consent for minors), limits public funding of abortion, and prohibits gender transition procedures for minors, with exceptions for specific medical conditions.
measures.againstMeans: A no vote leaves the 2024 amendment in place, so abortion stays available through fetal viability, and does not prohibit gender transition procedures for minors.

measures.title: Amendment 6 (Initiative petition constitutional amendment)
measures.summary: Would make the initiative and referendum process a fundamental right in the constitution and allow courts to revise ballot summaries through lawsuits. It would bar the legislature from weakening initiative or referendum powers, and from changing or repealing voter-approved initiatives without at least 80% of each chamber and a referral back to voters. Current signature and simple-majority requirements would stay the same.
measures.forMeans: A yes vote bars the legislature from directly changing laws passed by initiative. Any change would need at least 80% of each chamber and would go back to voters. It also restricts laws that limit initiatives and referenda and keeps current signature and simple-majority requirements.
measures.againstMeans: A no vote leaves the current constitutional provisions on initiatives and referenda unchanged.

measures.title: Amendment 7 (Legislatively referred constitutional amendment, SS SCS SJR 95)
measures.summary: Would create the "Show-Me Prosperity Fund," a permanent public endowment to support state government, and bar the legislature from spending it until the State Treasurer certifies that its earnings could replace state-imposed taxes. Those taxes would then be eliminated. Yearly spending from the fund would be capped at 3% of its average value, and the legislature could raise revenue if the fund failed.
measures.forMeans: A yes vote adds the Show-Me Prosperity Fund to the constitution, with the goal of eliminating state-imposed taxes once its investment earnings are high enough. It limits spending from the fund and bars bringing back eliminated taxes unless the fund becomes insolvent or falls short.
measures.againstMeans: A no vote means the constitution is not amended to create the endowment fund.

measures.title: Amendment 8 (Legislatively referred constitutional amendment, CCS HCS SS SJR 87)
measures.summary: Would put into the constitution the requirement that each county elect a sheriff every four years, which state law already requires, along with sheriffs' duties. An elected sheriff could be removed only through a writ of quo warranto brought by the Attorney General.
measures.forMeans: A yes vote requires counties to elect a sheriff every four years and puts sheriffs' duties, now set by state law, into the constitution. An elected sheriff could be removed only through a quo warranto action started by the Attorney General.
measures.againstMeans: A no vote leaves the constitution unchanged, and current state laws on electing sheriffs, their duties, and their removal stay in effect unless changed by law.

measures.title: Proposition A (Referendum on House Bill No. 1, 2025 Second Extraordinary Session)
measures.summary: Asks voters whether to approve the legislature's 2025 law that repeals Missouri's existing congressional district map and replaces it with new boundaries.
measures.forMeans: A yes vote approves House Bill No. 1, which redraws Missouri's congressional district boundaries.
measures.againstMeans: A no vote keeps the congressional district boundaries enacted in 2022.

measures.title: Constitutional Measure No. 1 – 60% vote to approve constitutional amendments
measures.summary: Referred by the Legislature (HCR 3003). Proposed amendments to the North Dakota Constitution, whether referred by the Legislature or started by citizen petition, would need at least 60% of the vote to pass. It amends Article III, Section 9 and Article IV, Section 16.
measures.forMeans: A yes vote means future constitutional amendments would need at least 60% voter approval to take effect.
measures.againstMeans: A no vote means constitutional amendments would still pass with a simple majority of votes.

measures.title: Initiated Constitutional Measure No. 2 – Free school breakfast and lunch
measures.summary: Placed on the ballot by citizen petition. Public school districts, public schools and public charter schools would have to give enrolled students one breakfast and one lunch each school day at no cost. Nonpublic and tribal schools could choose to take part. The state would reimburse schools at 100% of current free-meal rates, adjusted for inflation, paid from the Legacy Earnings Fund if the Legislature does not name another funding source. The Secretary of State's analysis estimates the cost at $124.3 million to $134.3 million for the 2027–2029 biennium.
measures.forMeans: A yes vote adds a section to the state constitution requiring free school breakfast and lunch for public school students, with state reimbursement to schools.
measures.againstMeans: A no vote leaves the constitution unchanged, so free school meals would not be required by the constitution.

measures.title: Constitutional Amendment A
measures.summary: This amendment changes how proposed constitutional amendments are published. Instead of being printed in newspapers, they would be published for the 60 days right before the general election in a way set by state law.
measures.forMeans: A FOR vote removes the newspaper publication requirement from the constitution. State law would then have the Lieutenant Governor post the full text of proposed amendments and other ballot questions from the Legislature on the Utah Public Notice Website and the Lieutenant Governor's website for the 60 days before the general election.
measures.againstMeans: An AGAINST vote keeps the constitution's current requirement that proposed constitutional amendments be published in newspapers before the election.

measures.title: Constitutional Amendment B
measures.summary: This amendment would require citizen-proposed laws (initiatives) that raise taxes compared to current law to win at least 60% of the vote, instead of a simple majority.
measures.forMeans: A FOR vote means a citizen initiative voted on after November 1, 2026 that creates a new tax, expands or raises an existing tax, or makes a property tax rate go down less than it would under current law would need at least 60% voter approval to pass.
measures.againstMeans: An AGAINST vote keeps the current rule: a citizen initiative passes with a simple majority of the votes cast on it, including initiatives that raise taxes.

measures.title: Initiative Measure No. IP26-645 (state and local taxes)
measures.summary: This measure would repeal the 9.9% state tax on yearly individual income over $1,000,000 that the Legislature passed in 2026 (ESSB 6346). It would also ban taxes measured by or placed on individual income, and define "income."
measures.forMeans: A yes vote repeals the 9.9% tax on individual income over $1,000,000 before it starts in 2028. It also adds a law banning state and local taxes on individual income.
measures.againstMeans: A no vote keeps the 9.9% tax on individual income over $1,000,000, which starts in calendar year 2028, and does not add the income-tax ban.

measures.title: Initiative Measure No. IL26-001 (parental rights relating to children in public school)
measures.summary: This measure would repeal the Legislature's 2025 changes to the state law that lists the rights of parents and guardians of public-school children (RCW 28A.605.005). The law would go back to the version first enacted through Initiative to the Legislature 2081 in 2024.
measures.forMeans: A yes vote repeals the 2025 changes and restores the parents' rights law as the Legislature first passed it in 2024 under Initiative 2081.
measures.againstMeans: A no vote keeps the parents' rights law as the Legislature amended it in 2025.

measures.title: Initiative Measure No. IL26-638 (participation in athletics at K-12 schools)
measures.summary: This measure would bar students the measure defines as "biologically male" from competing in K-12 school sports or events designated for female students only. Students would need a form signed by their health care provider verifying their biological sex. It would apply to public schools and to private schools in WIAA or similar organizations.
measures.forMeans: A yes vote bars students defined as biologically male from interschool sports designated for female students only, and requires provider-signed sex verification to take part in those sports.
measures.againstMeans: A no vote leaves the current rules in place, under which school sports must not discriminate on the basis of sex or gender identity.

53.measuresNote: There are three statewide initiatives this year. The full text, explanatory statements, fiscal impact statements, and arguments for and against are in the official state Voters' Pamphlet at sos.wa.gov/elections.

paxton.name: Ken Paxton
paxton.summary: Ken Paxton has been Texas attorney general since 2015. Before that he served 10 years in the Texas House and two years in the Texas Senate, representing the McKinney area. He won the Republican nomination for U.S. Senate over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, was impeached by the Texas House in 2023 and was acquitted on all charges by the Texas Senate.

positions.stance: Supports permanently repealing the federal gas tax. Supports keeping regulations on the oil and gas industry low and says more U.S. production will lower prices.
Supports more data center development in Texas with conditions, saying there is "plenty of open space" for them. Has called his position "a yes with conditions."
Said building roads and barriers in Big Bend is "not smart border security" and said he "fully supports" the federal decision to pause construction.
In a leaked recording of a private fundraiser, suggested he would support cuts to federal benefit programs to reduce the national deficit.
Supports a "pro-growth" regulatory framework for cryptocurrency and wants the U.S. to lead in digital assets.
Backs the president's actions on Iran; says he will decide on funding after getting more intelligence.
Opposes it; as attorney general he extended the state ban to mental health providers.
Has sued Dallas over marijuana decriminalization; no direct comment found on Texas THC rules.

history: Texas Attorney General, 2015–present
Texas Senate, 2 years (2013–2015)
Texas House, 10 years (2003–2013), McKinney area
Impeached by the Texas House in 2023; acquitted on all charges by the Texas Senate
Republican nominee for U.S. Senate, 2026

talarico.name: James Talarico
talarico.occupation: State representative; former middle school teacher
talarico.summary: James Talarico is a Democratic state representative from Austin, now in his fourth term in the Texas House, and a former middle school teacher in San Antonio ISD. He won the March 2026 Democratic primary for U.S. Senate over U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett. In the November 3, 2026 general election he faces Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Libertarian Ted Brown.

positions.stance: Proposes suspending federal taxes on gasoline and diesel to lower fuel costs.
Says data centers should pay for their own electricity infrastructure, lose their tax exemptions, and have less impact on local communities. Criticizes tax breaks given to data center companies.
Says he would support passing a war powers resolution to stop the war with Iran, arguing it has left both countries worse off.
Opposes the border wall in Big Bend, which he calls a 'monument to corruption.' Released a border security plan and has criticized both Biden-era border policies and the wall.
Asked about a federal ban on gender transition care for minors, said: 'I do not support gender reassignment surgery for minors.'
Supports legal, regulated adult-use marijuana, with tax revenue going to public safety and health programs.
Says he would vote 'to repeal these crazy tariffs,' arguing they raise costs for families.
Proposes banning members of Congress from trading individual stocks and setting term limits of six House terms and two Senate terms.
Said on Fox News: 'I oppose trans athletes playing in girls' sports if it endangers safety or fairness.'

ted-brown.name: Ted Brown
ted-brown.summary: Ted Brown is the Libertarian Party nominee for U.S. Senate in Texas. He joined the Libertarian Party in 1979, chaired the Libertarian Party of California, and is now vice chair of the Libertarian Party of Travis County. He was the party's 2024 nominee for U.S. Senate in Texas and received more than 267,000 votes, a record for a Libertarian Senate candidate in the state.

positions.stance: Would repeal the federal gas tax entirely.
Generally opposes regulation, but sees merit in requiring power and water plans and in banning taxpayer subsidies and eminent domain for data centers.
Supports every war powers resolution and wants U.S. troops withdrawn from the Middle East. Proposes withdrawing the U.S. from foreign conflicts and alliances, including NATO.
Wants Congress to bar a wall in Big Bend and to stop further border wall construction.
Says the government has no place in medical decisions between doctors and patients and argues the issue is overblown. Does not advocate surgery for minors.
Wants cannabis removed from federal drug scheduling and past marijuana convictions expunged.
Says only Congress can set tariffs; supports free trade.
Proposes abolishing the federal income tax, the IRS and the Department of Education, and making deep spending cuts to address the national debt.
Proposes an Ellis Island-style legal immigration system.
Describes himself as a strong supporter of Second Amendment gun rights.

eckhardt.name: Sarah Eckhardt
eckhardt.summary: Sarah Eckhardt is the Democratic state senator for Texas Senate District 14 and has held the seat since 2020. Before that, she served as Travis County Judge and as a Travis County commissioner. She dropped her bid for Congressional District 10 in December 2025 to run for comptroller, won the Democratic nomination in the March 3, 2026 primary, and will face Republican Don Huffines on November 3, 2026.

positions.stance: Proposes auditing Texas' $1 billion Education Freedom Accounts voucher program, which the comptroller's office runs, to look at who receives the money and how it is spent.
Pledges to investigate and stop no-bid state contracts that she says go to wealthy donors, and to root out government corruption.

positions.topic: Role and independence of the office
positions.stance: Says the comptroller should act as a government watchdog, run an independent office, and give Texans and lawmakers clearer information about how state money is spent.
Proposes using the office to report how much it costs Texas to refuse Medicaid expansion.
Has backed a moratorium on data center development.
Opposes a change that requires proof of legal immigration status to get a professional license.
Argues that the comptroller's office review of water fluoridation under Huffines is a misuse of state resources.
Argues that the comptroller's school spending review goes beyond the agency's authority, and says foreign workers and library books fall outside the review's scope.

faizi.name: Shehla Faizi
faizi.summary: Shehla Faizi is the Green Party nominee for Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts in the November 3, 2026 general election. She was nominated at the Green Party convention held April 11, 2026. She is running against Don Huffines (R), Sarah Eckhardt (D) and V. Alonzo Echavarria-Garza (L).

positions.stance: Opposes the Texas school voucher program. Cites data showing that most applicants already attended private schools and asks why tax dollars are going into private hands.
Pledges no tax breaks for data centers. Calls for more transparency from the comptroller's office on data center construction, saying there is no solid data on the job benefits of AI data centers.

Pledges unbiased state contracts. Says she would stop enforcing the state anti-boycott law that requires state contractors to pledge in writing not to take part in the BDS movement against Israel, and supports repealing anti-BDS laws.

positions.topic: Role and independence of the office
positions.stance: Says the comptroller should answer to the people, not party bosses or big donors. Says she accepts no billionaire, PAC or lobbyist money, and calls money in politics the biggest challenge facing Texas.
Proposes billboards about the state budget, modeled on TxDOT's road-safety billboards. Calls for all content on the comptroller's website to be available in Spanish.
Pledges that no taxpayer dollars will go to foreign bonds. Says Texas should divest from Israeli bonds and redirect its $280 million investment to Texas.
Campaign pledge: 'Texas Sheriffs for Texans - not ICE.'

tucker.occupation: Rancher on his family's ranch in Lampasas; fair trade organizer for the Trade Justice Education Fund; Secretary of the Texas Farmers Union
tucker.summary: Clayton Tucker, 35, is a fifth-generation Texan from Lampasas who works on his family's RX Ranch and is Secretary of the Texas Farmers Union. He ran unopposed in the March 3, 2026 Democratic primary and won the nomination with about 1.92 million votes. He faces Republican Nate Sheets in the November 3, 2026 general election for Texas Commissioner of Agriculture, an open seat after incumbent Sid Miller lost the Republican primary.

positions.stance: Proposes issuing 'Ag Impact Studies' on Day 1 that would require data centers to disclose their water and power use. Also proposes 'Ag Development Districts' so local communities can push back against data center projects.
Proposes requiring that public school lunches be made and processed in Texas. Supports removing harmful chemicals from food.
Supports stopping the spread of microplastics and regulating chemicals such as PFAS.

Supports breaking up corporate monopolies in agriculture, naming companies such as Tyson Foods and John Deere. Wants to make it easier for young farmers to stay in agriculture and to preserve family farms.
Lists lowering the cost of food among his campaign priorities.
Says his focus as commissioner would be removing the 'thievin elite' from the department and staying out of cultural fights.

His attorneys asked the Texas GOP to review whether Sheets meets the legal qualifications for the office. Tucker argues beekeeping does not count under the ag code, though he says he would probably support changing the law to include it.

Says he has written 11 bills to introduce if elected, including veterans-related legislation. Said he was undecided on the Major Richard Star Act and the Take Care of America's Veterans Act until he could review where the funding goes.

Would support or introduce War Powers Resolutions requiring Congress to approve further military action. Would use appropriations to withhold money for unauthorized operations, and would back bipartisan legislation barring funds to occupy or annex Greenland.

il-governor-and-lieutenant-governor-jb-p.name: JB Pritzker
il-governor-and-lieutenant-governor-jb-p.summary: JB Pritzker is the Democratic Governor of Illinois, first elected in 2018 and reelected in 2022, and is running for a third term in the November 3, 2026 general election. He had no opponent in the March 17, 2026 Democratic primary, and his running mate for Lieutenant Governor is Deputy Governor Christian Mitchell. His general election opponents are Republican Darren Bailey, whose running mate is Aaron Del Mar, and Independent Collin Corbett.

positions.stance: Says school and state public safety pension funding is at record levels and that school boards and local governments, which control property taxes, now have room to lower them. Cites police and fire pension consolidation as easing property tax pressure.

Signed a nearly $56 billion FY2027 budget that includes new business taxes. Says his administration has passed eight balanced budgets, paid down more than $12 billion in debt, and earned 12 credit upgrades.
Says he has never raised individual income, corporate income, or sales taxes. Lists lowering the tax burden on family farms and cutting income taxes for working families as third-term priorities.
Supports more electric generation capacity and clean baseload power, including new nuclear. Cites energy assistance for families earning up to $99,000 and $800 million in required utility rebates.
Opposes taxpayers paying for a $3 billion stadium. Wants the Bears to stay in Illinois and supports the state providing basic infrastructure for a new stadium.

Halted state tax incentives for new data centers starting July 1, 2026. Proposes requiring data centers to supply their own clean energy, limit water use, and sign transparent agreements with local communities.
Supports changing incentives so they must produce a positive return for taxpayers. Says companies that don't deliver the jobs and investment they promised shouldn't receive the incentives.
Says Illinois schools are better funded than ever and agrees schools need more money. Says school funding must stay sustainable over the long term.
Proposes a housing plan to lower costs by building much more housing, including zoning law changes. Cites down payment help already given to first-time homebuyers.

Defends the state's criminal justice reforms, says Bailey would bring back a system where violent criminals can buy their way out of jail, and supports violence intervention, law enforcement, and behavioral health funding.

His office investigated conditions in ICE detention. He says it found more than 1,000 credible allegations of abuse, including inadequate nutrition and sexual abuse.

Opposes the U.S. war in Iran, saying it was launched without evidence of an imminent threat, without clear objectives and before diplomacy was exhausted. His campaign cites six votes he cast for war powers resolutions.
Says Georgia's six-week abortion ban takes away women's autonomy and puts their health at risk. Sponsored a bill to prohibit government restrictions on abortion.
In 2021, sponsored a bill to raise the federal minimum wage to $15 over five years.
Says Israeli forces violated the law of armed conflict and international humanitarian law in Gaza. Says whether genocide occurred is for the International Criminal Court to decide.

mi-u-s-senate-walter-p-kristy.occupation: Accountant and tax preparer; former teacher
mi-u-s-senate-walter-p-kristy.summary: Walter P. Kristy is the Natural Law Party nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan on the November 3, 2026 general election ballot. He is registered with the Federal Election Commission as a Natural Law Party Senate candidate (FEC ID S6MI00590). He says the party lets him run an independent campaign with no party control over his positions.

positions.stance: Supports abortion rights and calls himself pro-choice. Says he hopes society can help all women see having a child as a positive choice in any circumstances.
Supports an individual's right to own a weapon to protect themselves and their family.
Pledges to protect the civil liberties in the Bill of Rights. Says he is concerned about how data collected through data centers is used.

Says heads of businesses that break pollution laws belong in jail. Supports funding cleanup of toxic chemicals and plastic waste from food, soil, water and air, and requiring companies to internalize their environmental costs.
Proposes helping food producers shift to organic, regenerative agriculture to increase biodiversity, produce food free of toxins and improve the water cycle.
Supports postponing new data centers until citizens have adequate access to electricity and drinkable water. Says data centers should need approval from the communities where they are built.
Supports upgrading the power grid. Says providing utilities should not be a for-profit business.

Says he would hold discussions on issues with Michiganders and bring the results to the Senate. Pledges to push for legislation that serves the whole community, not special interests, and to act as a check on the executive branch.

ak-united-states-senator-mary-peltola.summary: Mary Peltola is a Yup'ik Alaskan and former tribal judge. She represented Alaska's at-large U.S. House district from 2022 to 2025 and was the first Alaska Native member of Congress. She lost re-election to the House in 2024 and is now the Democratic nominee running against incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in the November 3, 2026 general election.

positions.stance: Argues that the war with Iran has raised fuel and living costs in Alaska, saying Alaskans are "being priced out" because of the war. Criticizes Sullivan's support for the war.
Says that if elected she would work to speed up federal reviews of resource development projects under laws such as the Endangered Species Act and NEPA.
Calls for more NOAA funding and blames federal budget cuts for problems in the fishing industry. Argues that federal fisheries policy should focus on wild-caught fish rather than farmed fish.
Opposes cuts to NOAA and to the federal fisheries science workforce that came through the Elon Musk-led cost-cutting initiative.

Introduced legislation to expand the lands available for Alaska Native land selections.

ak-governor-lieutenant-governor-dave-bro.summary: Dave Bronson is a Republican and was the mayor of Anchorage from July 2021 to July 2024. He entered the governor's race on October 2, 2025. Proposes a review of every state department and cutting programs that cannot show results. Says he would not cut troopers, classroom teachers, ferries or rural infrastructure, and would expand public safety and career and technical education.
Says developing Alaska's resources will create good-paying jobs and bring royalty revenue to the state.

ak-governor-lieutenant-governor-jonathan.name: Jonathan S. "JKT" Kreiss-Tomkins
ak-governor-lieutenant-governor-jonathan.summary: Jonathan S. "JKT" Kreiss-Tomkins is a Democrat from Sitka who served in the Alaska House of Representatives from 2013 to 2023. He is running for governor with Zac Johnson as his running mate to succeed term-limited Gov. Mike Dunleavy. He advanced from the August 18, 2026 nonpartisan top-four primary to the ranked-choice general election.

positions.stance: Supports fully funding and forward-funding public schools. Says the current governor has defunded schools for nearly a decade. Supports getting cell phones out of classrooms.
Opposes a constitutional amendment to have public education funding follow the child. Says he supports freedom of education, but not publicly funded freedom of education.
Supports amending the state constitution to restrict Permanent Fund spending and prevent overspending of the fund.
Opposes a $4,000 dividend this year, arguing it would drain the fund within decades. Supports a smaller dividend he says is sustainable.
Calls for a "fish first" governor: reducing bycatch, putting Alaskans rather than Lower 48 trawl interests in charge of fisheries, and stopping the Pebble Mine to protect salmon habitat.
Supports protecting Medicaid expansion and expanding telehealth.
Proposes lowering electric bills by making utilities cooperate and by building renewable energy. Supports cutting red tape to build more homes and easing regulations on new childcare providers.

ak-governor-lieutenant-governor-bernadet.name: Bernadette M. Wilson
ak-governor-lieutenant-governor-bernadet.summary: Bernadette M. Wilson is a Republican business owner from Anchorage. She was born in Kenai and owns Denali Disposal. She announced her campaign for governor on May 13, 2025, and has never held elected office. She advanced from the August 18, 2026 nonpartisan top-four primary to the November 3 general election, and her running mate for lieutenant governor is Mike Shower.

positions.stance: Supports paying the full statutory (formula) dividend, about $3,800 this year. She says lawmakers should 'follow the formula' and was the only debate candidate to back a formula dividend.
Says the dividend formula creates an obligation to Alaskans that should be repaid, even if that means breaking the current spending limit on the Permanent Fund.
Proposes an audit of state government to find efficiencies and tasks that can be automated, plus a yearly 'state of the budget address.'
Has said she would shrink the state workforce to deal with the budget. She argues Alaska has one of the highest numbers of government employees per capita.
Supports moving energy and mining projects forward in partnership with the Trump administration and argues her Democratic opponent would block them.
In her official election statement, she says Alaska's education ranks near the bottom and pledges that 'our children will attend the best schools.'
Endorsed by Alaska Right to Life Action. The group said she was the only candidate for governor who met with it on its priorities, including ending state funding for abortion.

az-governor-and-lieutenant-governor-kati.name: Katie Hobbs
az-governor-and-lieutenant-governor-kati.summary: Katie Hobbs is the Democratic Governor of Arizona and has held the office since January 2023. Before that she was Arizona Secretary of State and served in the state legislature. She won the 2026 Democratic nomination without an opponent and is running for a second term with former Mesa Mayor John Giles as her running mate.

positions.stance: Opposes federal Medicaid cuts and says Arizona cannot absorb them. She rejected state GOP budget proposals that would have cut Medicaid.
Supports adding oversight and accountability to the Empowerment Scholarship Account program, including a way to claw back unused funds. She calls the current program a "billion-dollar boondoggle."

Says border security has been a focus since her first day in office. Started Operation Desert Guardian, a multi-agency effort against cartel activity, and says she works with the federal government on border security.
Arizona, under her administration, joined Nevada's lawsuit against the U.S. Interior Department to block federal cuts to Lower Basin Colorado River water supplies.
Her campaign says she will work across party lines to cut taxes, erase medical debt for nearly 700,000 people, secure the border and protect water.
Criticized delays in federal SNAP benefits during the 2025 shutdown, saying nearly 900,000 Arizonans rely on the program. She considered declaring a state of emergency.
Opposes Proposition 144 on the 2026 ballot.
Chose not to debate Andy Biggs. Her campaign says face-to-face engagement with Arizonans works better than a debate stage.

az-governor-and-lieutenant-governor-andy.summary: Andy Biggs is a Republican who has represented Arizona's 5th Congressional District in the U.S. House since 2017. He won the Republican primary for governor in 2026. He is running in the November 3, 2026 general election with Sine Kerr as his lieutenant governor candidate.

positions.stance: Supports eliminating Arizona's state income tax and says he would take the first step toward that goal. Also supports working with local entities to reduce property taxes.
Says affordability is the top concern he hears from voters. Proposes codifying the repeal of what he calls Gov. Hobbs' housing moratorium on new single-family homes in fast-growing areas.

Says water is the issue he is asked about most and argues the state cannot conserve its way out of shortages. He points to a bill he introduced in Congress for $19 billion in federal water infrastructure funding.
Opposes additional tax breaks and subsidies for data centers. Says data centers should generate their own energy, avoid straining the power grid and water supply, and recycle water.
Proposes lowering fuel prices by reducing Arizona's reliance on California for fuel and increasing supply from other sources.
Supports ending medical mandates and 'ensuring vaccine freedom.' Has released a health policy platform aligned with Make America Healthy Again (MAHA).
Lists support for Arizona's Empowerment Scholarship Account (ESA) program among his priorities as governor.

ar-u-s-senate-hallie-shoffner.occupation: Farmer; former manager of her family's rice and soybean farm
ar-u-s-senate-hallie-shoffner.summary: Hallie Shoffner is a farmer from northeast Arkansas who managed her family's rice and soybean farm and a seed company, and founded an agricultural food hub. She launched her campaign for U.S. Senate in July 2025. She won the March 3, 2026 Democratic primary over Lewisville Mayor Ethan Dunbar with about 78% of the vote and faces Republican incumbent Tom Cotton and Libertarian Jeff Wadlin on November 3, 2026.

positions.stance: Supports farm policy that encourages growing a wider range of crops and public-private partnerships to build processing facilities near farm communities. Calls for passing a Farm Bill.

Says too much farmland consolidation by corporations, private equity and wealthy people should be treated as an antitrust violation. Proposes farmland trusts, low-interest loans for young farmers and taxes on large consolidators.

Supports expanding Medicare coverage, raising Medicaid reimbursement rates, and investing in telehealth, federally qualified health centers and more medical residencies. Says Medicaid is economic infrastructure for rural hospitals.

Says she has a "serious problem" with ICE's level of funding and supports putting resources toward the immigration court backlog. Says undocumented immigrants should be deported if they commit a crime with a victim, not solely for being undocumented.
Would support ending the war in Iran and has criticized what the war costs Americans.
Supports federal AI regulation so products are vetted for consumer safety before reaching the market. Says data centers should sign community development agreements with local governments.
Campaign platform pledges to lower the cost of living, keep jobs in Arkansas, support workers and strengthen unions, and pay teachers and school staff more.

Would create an ongoing state funding stream for rental assistance and homelessness prevention, plus a public dashboard tracking state-funded units. Says people should not be allowed to stay on the street when offered shelter.

Points to his record of suing the first Trump administration more than 100 times as attorney general. Says he would take a similar approach as governor on issues such as immigration and environmental policy.
Voted for Proposition 36 (2024). Says he would fully fund its provisions and make sure defendants receive court-mandated drug treatment to avoid jail time.
Says he will protect Californians from federal Medicaid cuts.

Proposes to 'bring back the starter home' by cutting fees and building rules for small single-family homes, plus a state loan program for first-time buyers. Would bar CEQA lawsuits used to stop construction.

Says street camping is illegal and that police should help clear all encampments. Proposes funding sober housing and recovery centers with addiction and mental health treatment, and overhauling state homelessness spending.

Proposes rolling back state climate mandates, ending rules that require utilities to buy solar and wind power, and allowing more natural gas production. Also proposes a volunteer tree-planting and forest restoration program.
Endorsed by President Trump. Says he expects a cooperative relationship with the president that would help California get more federal assistance.
Supports school choice through education savings accounts and ending teacher tenure. Proposes banning smartphone use for children under 14 and pausing AI use in schools until summer 2027.
Says state spending has doubled in ten years. Proposes spending cuts, ending the high-speed rail project, reducing bureaucracy and acting against Medi-Cal fraud to offset his tax cuts.

co-united-states-senator-adam-withrow.summary: Adam Withrow is the Unity Party nominee for U.S. Senate in Colorado on the November 3, 2026 general election ballot. He describes himself as a working-class candidate, not a politician, and has worked as a ranch hand, certified nursing assistant, cook, contractor and detention officer. He is running against Democratic incumbent John Hickenlooper, Republican Mark Baisley, and three other minor-party candidates.

positions.stance: Proposes a federal living wage tied to the Consumer Price Index so wages rise with prices. He would phase it in by industry based on gross receipts and profitability. He calls raising wages his first priority.
Calls for a unilateral U.S. declaration of peace and an end to what he calls a global military empire, while keeping national self-defense. Opposes U.S. involvement in 'wars of choice.'
Says fossil fuels are finite and 'obsolete' as a basis for future building, while acknowledging continued use. Supports starting a transition to newer energy technology now.
Supports redesigning the health care system to cover everyone. Argues that 'healthcare for all' would cost less than half of the defense budget.
Says lobbyist and donor money amounts to 'legal bribery.' Says he does not seek big donors and is not beholden to either major party.
Proposes putting each Senate vote to Colorado voters first and casting his vote the way they decide.
Supports working toward moving data centers into orbit. Lists energy, water and AI among his top concerns.

He is running for public office for the first time. Proposes a review of agency spending, contracts, vacant positions and duplicative programs. Would make departments justify their spending and would rebid contracts competitively. Puts public safety, education, infrastructure and essential services first.

Proposes faster residential permitting, a review of mandates that raise construction costs, more relief for seniors and more competition in property insurance. Would require cost-benefit analysis before new regulations.
Supports law enforcement. Says he would focus resources on violent crime, fentanyl, trafficking and repeat offenders.
Proposes audits of executive agencies and a public dashboard showing state spending, contracts and agency performance.

co-governor-and-lieutenant-governor-phil.summary: Phil Weiser is Colorado's attorney general, an office he first won in 2018. He won the Democratic primary for governor on June 30, 2026, beating U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet. On July 22, 2026, he named Jefferson County Commissioner Lesley Dahlkemper as his running mate for lieutenant governor.

positions.stance: Has set a goal of building 40,000 new starter homes. Says he would work with local governments to speed up permits and lower permit fees, and would push for wider use of modular housing.

Says he would lead an effort to change TABOR so the state can pay for key investments. Argues the state lacks enough money for major services, especially K-12 education, but would also cut spending that audits flagged as questionable.

Says he would sign a bill removing the second union-security vote required under the Colorado Labor Peace Act, which he calls antiquated. Says he would work with employers and unions to try to reach consensus.

Says Colorado should lead in protecting natural resources while keeping energy affordable, using targeted rules aimed at the most damaging emission sources, and says he would enforce environmental laws.
His governing blueprint proposes reducing the number of inmates who re-offend, which he says would also lower state costs.
Said at the Colorado Chamber forum that he is more willing than Gov. Polis to regulate emerging technologies and social media to protect residents.

Says Flock license-plate camera systems raise serious Fourth Amendment concerns. Would oppose any expansion or unrestricted use of them.
Says the Attorney General should closely monitor mergers and other antitrust concerns.
Supports small, efficient government that uses tax dollars wisely, with solutions tailored to different regions of the state.

co-governor-and-lieutenant-governor-erik.summary: Erik Underwood is the Approval Voting Party nominee for Colorado governor in the Nov. 3, 2026 general election, with Frank Atwood as his running mate for lieutenant governor. He calls himself an independent Democrat and says he ran at the Democratic state assembly in spring 2026, finished second, and did not reach the threshold for the primary ballot. He then got a ballot spot through the Approval Voting Party.

positions.stance: Proposes state-backed home loans at 2.75% through a new housing division, state-owned homes, converting empty office buildings into affordable housing, housing zones to keep rents down, and rent freezes where needed.
Plans to prepare a ballot measure to eliminate TABOR. Says Medicaid grows about 9% a year while TABOR lets the budget grow about 3%.
Proposes saving money by ending private prison contracts, cutting outside consultants, and using the state's buying power to lower prescription drug costs, instead of cutting services.
Supports higher taxes on extremely wealthy residents.
Opposes criminalizing people for sleeping in parks. Proposes more shelters, mobile crisis teams, mental-health care, addiction treatment, and transitional housing.
Says Colorado's protections are the Colorado River Compact and prior appropriation. Says he will not accept a river deal where Colorado agriculture is the only water that gets cut.

Proposes a moratorium on data centers starting his first day in office because of their water and power use. Says he would not approve AI data centers that use millions of gallons of water for cooling.
Would not expand oil and gas development beyond current levels. Opposes fracking near reservoirs, drinking water, and wildlife areas. Says communities should decide which developments they accept.
His priorities include universal health care, child care support, and free college and trade school.
Supports lowering the voting age to 16 and plans to propose a bill to do so in his first year.

Says he wants to reform TABOR through a grassroots, bottom-up effort that would include changes to the state tax system and to constitutional spending limits.
Says the structural deficit cannot be solved with temporary fixes, accounting maneuvers or across-the-board cuts to essential services, and that the structure of spending itself must change.
Said in an August 2026 debate that the jury is still out on data centers, and that he is worried about their water use.
Proposes help for rural hospitals.

de-u-s-senator-chris-coons.name: Chris Coons
de-u-s-senator-chris-coons.summary: Chris Coons is a Democrat who has represented Delaware in the U.S. Senate since winning a 2010 election, and he is running for another term. He won the Democratic primary on Sept. 15, 2026, beating Jeff Appelhans, Eric No-Trump Hansen and Mary Louve. In the Nov. 3 general election he faces Republican Dr. Michael "Mike" Katz.

positions.stance: Says his priorities are opportunity, security and justice: raising wages, protecting residents from threats abroad and at home, and rooting out corruption in Washington.
Says both parties share responsibility for deficits. Supports raising taxes on wealthy Americans and highly profitable corporations while giving relief to working families.
Supports raising the income cap on Social Security payroll taxes. Supports a bipartisan process to consider other changes to strengthen the program.
Defends the Affordable Care Act as a way to expand access to insurance and preventive care. Argues that better access to primary care can reduce costly emergency treatment.

Opposes the Trump administration's broad tariffs, arguing they raise prices for consumers and businesses, including Delaware's chemical, agriculture and port industries. Favors removing trade barriers.

Opposes the administration's conduct of the war with Iran, citing poor planning and too little consultation with Congress and allies. Calls for ending the conflict and reopening shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Supports continued U.S. support for Ukraine against Russia's invasion.
Supports keeping the Senate filibuster. Is open to some reforms, especially for voting rights legislation.
Supports border security combined with more accountability for federal immigration enforcement and legal pathways for qualifying immigrants.
Supports responsible AI development, with an emphasis on safeguards and on how data centers affect local communities.

Supports prescription drug pricing reform that protects innovation, more rural health funding for Kent and Sussex counties, lower insurance premiums, and making mental health part of primary care.

Supports fully funding military readiness and modernizing the armed forces. Also supports protecting veterans' benefits, reducing VA disability claim backlogs and expanding telehealth for rural veterans.
Says his focus in the Senate would be lowering the cost of living, fixing the health care system and making the federal government more fiscally responsible.

Opposes abortion. Told the Honolulu Star-Advertiser in 2022 that as governor he would sign legislation overturning abortion rights if it reached his desk.

Says his administration made Idaho the least regulated state in the nation (2026 State of the State).
Supports the State of Idaho's expanded partnership with the federal government to speed up forest management across the state.

id-governor-john-r-stegner.summary: John R. Stegner is a retired Idaho Supreme Court justice who spent 25 years as a judge in Idaho, first as a district judge in Latah County starting in 1997 and then on the Supreme Court from 2018 until he retired in 2023. He filed as an independent candidate for governor on February 27, 2026, and the Idaho Secretary of State lists his filing as approved for the November 3, 2026 general election. He formally launched his campaign on July 7, 2026, saying he is running to restore confidence in Idaho government.

positions.stance: Opposes the Idaho Parental Choice Tax Credit (HB 93). Says it is unconstitutional to fund private and homeschool students while public schools are not adequately funded, and says his first act as governor would be to try to challenge it in court.

Says Idaho has a "solemn obligation" to fund public schools and that current leaders are not meeting it. Lists fulfilling the constitutional duty to fund public education as one of his top three priorities.

Supports Proposition 1, the ballot initiative to restore abortion rights in Idaho, and says he would carry it out if it passes. As a justice in 2023, he wrote that the Idaho Constitution protects a fundamental right to end a pregnancy.
Opposes HJR 4, which would let only the Legislature legalize marijuana or other drugs, and HJR 6, which would make English Idaho's official language. Says he will vote against both.

Opposes the agreement to host a federal Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus that would require Idaho to accept out-of-state spent fuel. Argues Idaho could end up taking far more than a third of the nation's waste unless the plan is stopped now.

Says he would not have signed Idaho's 287(g) agreement with ICE. Argues the agency's conduct, including agents wearing masks and not wearing body cameras, should be reined in before Idaho enters such an agreement.
Lists keeping public lands in public hands as one of his top three priorities.
Criticizes the Legislature for cutting taxes and spending and for creating the private school tax credit. Says he would act independently and not give in to outside or political pressure.
Lists increasing access to medical care as one of his top three priorities.

mn-u-s-senator-michele-tafoya.summary: Michele Tafoya is a former NBC sideline reporter and four-time Emmy winner who later worked as a conservative commentator. She launched her Republican campaign in January 2026 for the open U.S. Senate seat left by retiring Sen. Tina Smith (D), with support from the NRSC. She is the Republican nominee in the November 3, 2026 general election.

positions.stance: Says Washington is overspending. Proposes protecting Social Security, Medicare and national defense by cutting spending and waste, fraud and abuse, and opposes tax increases.

In the MPR debate she did not say whether she would support higher taxes or benefit cuts to keep Social Security solvent. She said solving it needs independent senators willing to work across party lines.

Supports keeping Rural Health Transformation funding for Minnesota. Proposes stopping overcharging by hospitals and drug companies, limiting insurers' use of prior authorization to deny seniors' care, and fighting Medicare/Medicaid fraud.
Supports strong border security and the rule of law, plus legal pathways for high-skilled workers, guest workers and immigrants who follow the law and assimilate.

Opposes permanent high tariffs and supports using short-term tariff leverage to secure new trade deals. Says the USMCA should already have been renewed and that she wishes the President had taken a different approach with Canada.

Calls herself a 'pro-choice Republican' and supports 'reasonable access' to abortion in the first 12 weeks. Opposes taxpayer funding of abortion and Minnesota's current abortion-access law, and would confirm 'strict-constructionist' judges.
Says fraud reform is a central reason she is running. Proposes using the Senate's investigative and oversight powers to address Minnesota's public-program fraud cases.
Says she stands with Israel and disputes calling events in Gaza a genocide.
Welcomes data center investment if developers are open about local costs and impacts, and says local landowners and residents should have a say.

mt-united-states-senator-kyle-austin.summary: Kyle Austin is a pharmacist from Billings who owns the pharmacy business Pharm406. He ran twice as a Republican for Montana's eastern U.S. House seat, then switched to the Libertarian Party. He won the June 2, 2026 Libertarian primary for U.S. Senate with 53.3% of the vote over Tom Jandron and is the party's nominee in the November 3 general election.

positions.stance: Says the War Powers Resolution of 1973 should be enforced. Supports the president being able to act quickly, with troops withdrawn within 60 days unless Congress authorizes further force.
Proposes a plan he calls "Healthcare 2.0" to overhaul the health system. He says it would remove annual deductibles, lower premiums and raise payments to providers at no added cost to taxpayers.

Says his "Healthcare 2.0" plan would create one set of rules and require payers to pay providers what they are worth. He has said recent changes to Medicaid could cause eligible Montanans to lose coverage.
Proposes working to lower interest rates, reducing barriers that raise construction costs, eliminating tariffs on building supplies, and promoting responsible logging and lumber mills in Montana.

Proposes cutting what he calls wasteful federal spending and government overreach, deregulating businesses and lowering taxes for everyone. He has also said he is concerned about the size of the federal government and the national debt.
Says farmers and ranchers should be kept out of trade wars and supports zero tariffs on construction supplies. He has said President Trump's tariff policies are misdirected.

Supports a lawful, faster immigration system with stronger border security, more legal pathways and due process. Proposes asylum screenings within 7 days, a 30-day goal for final decisions, and more immigration judges.
Says there is no stopping AI and data centers but that safeguards are needed. He has suggested putting data centers in space or in the ocean.
Proposes individual trust funds so that a worker's contributions stay with that worker instead of paying current retirees. He says retirement money should be "your money, not the government's money."
Proposes overhauling the USDA, offering 0% USDA financing to farmers and ranchers, addressing what he calls market fraud, and supporting fertilizer plants in the U.S. to reduce reliance on imports.

positions.stance: Supports universal healthcare modeled on the military's TRICARE program, paid for by cutting administrative waste and drug middlemen. Supports protecting the Medicare and Medicaid payments that rural hospitals depend on.
Opposes ever selling public lands or opening them up for exploitation. Supports corner crossing.
Says she takes no corporate PAC money. Supports I-194, The Montana Plan, which she says would end dark money in Montana.
Supports abortion rights. Says the Supreme Court took away a constitutional right in 2022 and points to Montana voters adding reproductive rights to the state constitution.
Says she is a gun owner who carried a firearm professionally for 21 years, and that she respects firearm use for hunting, sport and family protection.
Opposes AI and large-scale data centers on public lands. Elsewhere, opposes them unless there are studies, full disclosure and protections in place.
Proposes funding wildfire prevention, drought protection for ranches, restoring clean-energy credits through co-ops (incentives, not mandates), and a border charge on foreign polluters.
Says she supports securing the border, fixing what she calls a broken immigration system, and treating people humanely.
Opposes blanket tariffs. Argues they act as a tax on groceries and cost Montana farmers their export markets.
Opposes the war with Iran, which she calls illegal and unauthorized by Congress. Says Congress should reclaim its war powers.

mt-united-states-senator-seth-bodnar.summary: Seth Bodnar is a former U.S. Army Special Forces officer and former General Electric executive who served as president of the University of Montana from 2018 until January 2026. He is on the November 3, 2026 ballot with Republican Kurt Alme, Democrat Alani Bankhead and Libertarian Kyle Austin.

positions.stance: Says declaring war is Congress's constitutional responsibility and argues that partisanship has led members of Congress to cede too much power to the executive branch.
Supports telehealth expansion and workforce incentives for rural health care. Opposes cuts to critical access hospitals and says he will defend Montana's Medicaid expansion.
Says the recent party-line budget bill will remove more than 30,000 Montanans from health coverage and cost rural hospitals more than $5 billion. Opposes cuts that would remove coverage.
Supports building more homes by cutting red tape, using tax incentives and fixing supply chains. Supports rules to stop private equity firms from buying large numbers of single-family homes.
Says tariffs should be strategic tools to open markets and protect key industries. Opposes the trade dispute with Canada and pledges to reassert Congress's authority over tariffs.

Supports strong borders, enforcement of immigration law and comprehensive immigration reform. Says enforcement must respect due process and opposes use of what he calls an unaccountable, masked force.
Supports strict federal guardrails so data centers cannot be built in Montana communities without community involvement, and to protect water supplies and electricity rates.
Describes himself as a strong supporter of reproductive freedom. Says a woman's health decisions should be between her, her doctor, her family and her faith.
Says protecting public lands is a top priority and calls them common ground where everyone can hunt, fish and recreate.
Says government has "no business" in Montanans' gun cabinets.

ne-governor-and-lt-governor-jim-pillen.summary: Jim Pillen, a Republican from Columbus, has been Nebraska's 41st governor since January 2023. He filed for reelection in January 2026 and won the May 12, 2026 Republican primary. His running mate is Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, and in the November 3 general election he faces Democrat Lynne Walz, Rick Beard (Legal Marijuana NOW), and Brett Lindstrom (America First).

positions.stance: Says he worked with the Legislature to pass historic income tax relief and that his administration is actively addressing what he calls the property tax crisis.
Supports parental school choice. Says Nebraska was the first state to opt in to the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit, which he says lets parents pick the school that fits their child best.
Cites a bell-to-bell cellphone ban in schools and a focus on making sure all children read at grade level as education priorities.
Says he wants to run government like a business by cutting spending and regulations, and that it is important to say no to more spending, programs, and government.
Says he has worked with legislators regardless of party to pass bills on education, taxes, and agriculture. Describes himself as a conservative Republican who supports less government and low taxes.
His reelection campaign video promotes rules on transgender athletes, which he described as keeping "men out of girls sports."
Issued executive orders for a 90-day pause on state diesel taxes for agriculture producers. Has also asked President Trump to impose a federal ban on diesel exports.
Supports Second Amendment rights and backs a 'stand your ground' law.

ne-governor-and-lt-governor-lynne-walz.summary: Lynne Walz of Fremont is a Realtor, small business owner, former teacher and former state senator for Nebraska Legislative District 15 (2017–2025). She formed an exploratory committee in November 2025, held a statewide listening tour and announced her campaign for governor on January 21, 2026. She won the Democratic nomination in the May 12, 2026 primary, and her running mate is farmer Ben Steffen.

positions.stance: Says she would sign an executive order on her first day in office so patients can get medical marijuana with a doctor's prescription. She would also replace Medical Cannabis Commission members who do not carry out the 2024 voter-approved law.
Calls property tax a major affordability issue and links it to the rising age of first-time homebuyers. She says property tax relief should get priority over social issues.
Proposes more collaboration and shared resources among local entities to lower costs. One example is businesses opening daycares, or nursing homes and daycares working together.
Says that on her first day as governor she would reject school voucher funds.
Says that on her first day as governor she would hire an independent auditor. She also says state officials should respect ballot measures that voters have passed.
Says the governor should focus on creating and attracting good-paying jobs, supporting public schools and lowering the cost of food and other daily expenses.

As a senator, voted against advancing the 2024 Sports and Spaces Act out of the Education Committee. She says the Nebraska School Activities Association already had policies in place, so the Legislature did not need to focus on the issue.
Says she will work with people of any party. She cites endorsements from four former Republican legislative colleagues.

Charvat III for the party's nomination in the May 12, 2026 primary and is on the November 3 general election ballot. Says new revenue from cannabis and hemp would let the state reduce property taxes and fix roads.
To close the state budget shortfall, says Nebraska must end tax breaks for corporations and the 'ultra-rich' and must not turn away federal dollars.
Wants to remove corporate, special-interest and political action committee (PAC) money from Nebraska politics, and calls this a central focus of his campaign.
Supports legalizing industrial hemp. Proposes using hemp to double Nebraska's biofuel production and to make cheaper building materials for housing.
Proposes pausing data center development for closer review and requiring closed-loop cooling systems.

ne-governor-and-lt-governor-brett-lindst.name: Brett Lindstrom
ne-governor-and-lt-governor-brett-lindst.summary: Brett Lindstrom of Omaha represented District 18 in the Nebraska Legislature from 2015 to 2023 and finished third in the 2022 Republican primary for governor. In 2026 he tried to qualify as a nonpartisan candidate for governor with running mate Mike Picard, but he fell short after the Secretary of State found many petition signatures invalid, many of them flagged as fraudulent. On Sept. 1, 2026, after the Nebraska Supreme Court cleared the new America First Party's recognition, he filed as the party's nominee for governor.

positions.stance: Proposes moving major property classes toward rolling valuation averaging to reduce swings in valuations. Proposes lowering schools' maximum operating levy from $1.05 to 50 cents per $100 of valuation over time, with more state aid as finances allow.
Proposes valuing farmland mostly on productive income (about 80% income, 20% market value) instead of 75% of market value. Supports keeping more of Nebraska's farm products processed in-state.

Says the current administration spent through a historic cash reserve, raided cash funds and made billions in commitments without a sustainable way to pay for them. Argues 'you cannot cut your way to prosperity, and you cannot spend your way to growth.'

Proposes that the state talk less about data centers by name and more about digital infrastructure, secure cloud services, computing capacity and cybersecurity. Supports protecting public power and expanding the electric grid ahead of demand.
Proposes building housing near existing jobs and infrastructure, recruiting former Nebraskans back to the state, and investing in regional growth hubs.
Supports coordinating K-12 schools, community colleges, apprenticeships and employers as one workforce pipeline. Supports finishing rural broadband deployment.
Says neither major party is willing to tell Nebraskans the truth. Says he is not running a protest or 'spoiler' campaign.

nv-governor-joe-lombardo.name: Joe Lombardo
nv-governor-joe-lombardo.summary: Joe Lombardo is the Republican governor of Nevada. He was elected in 2022 after serving as Clark County Sheriff. He is running for a second term in the November 3, 2026 general election.

positions.stance: Has pledged no new taxes and says he has kept that pledge since his first campaign. Opposes resetting property tax values.
Supports keeping Nevada's right-to-work law and opposes repealing it. Has said the system benefits the state's labor community.
Proposes a 12% increase in per-student funding over the biennium in his two-year budget plan. Has not committed to raising funding to the national average.
Supports holding back third graders who do not read at grade level. He brought the policy back in his 2023 education bill, AB400.
Supports requiring photo ID to vote. He backed the 2024 voter ID ballot question publicly and with money.
Has said he would personally support a 15-week limit. Says abortion rights are written into state law and should be left to Nevada voters.

His campaign says the state already has strong protections against shifting data center costs to ratepayers, with guidance set through the Public Utilities Commission. It gave no yes-or-no answer on a new law.
Vetoed a 2023 bill to cap corporate ownership of homes. His campaign gave no yes-or-no answer on new limits.
Proposes lowering the felony theft threshold from $1,200 to $750, as he called for in his 2025 State of the State address.
Supports the death penalty and opposes repealing it. He said in 2021 that it deters crime and is a solution for egregious crimes.

nv-governor-aaron-ford.name: Aaron Ford
nv-governor-aaron-ford.summary: Aaron Ford is Nevada's Democratic attorney general. Term limits bar him from running for that office again, so he is running for governor. He won the Democratic nomination in the June 9, 2026 primary, where his opponents included Washoe County Commissioner Alexis Hill, and faces Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo in the November 3, 2026 general election.

positions.stance: Says that as governor he would repeal Nevada's 'right-to-work' law, which bars requiring union membership as a condition of employment.
Supports a law requiring data centers to provide their own power instead of shifting costs to ratepayers; his campaign says he plans to introduce legislation to do that.
Opposes raising taxes, including resetting property tax values. His campaign said in August 2026 that he will not raise taxes.
Supports raising per-pupil K-12 funding to the national average, about $2 billion, without new taxes. Proposes growing the tax base by attracting businesses from financial and high-tax sectors.
Would not repeal the 'Read by Grade 3' law that holds back third graders who are not reading proficiently starting in 2028, but says he is open to adjustments.
Opposes a photo ID requirement to vote. Says there is not enough evidence of voter fraud in Nevada to justify one.
Supports enshrining abortion rights through 24 weeks in the Nevada Constitution. Pledges to protect abortion access and IVF.
Proposes limiting corporate investors from buying single-family homes, cracking down on landlords he calls predatory, and easing restrictions on new construction.
Opposes lowering the $1,200 felony theft threshold. As attorney general he testified in support of the 2019 bill AB236, which raised the threshold from $650.
Opposes the death penalty and says he would sign a bill repealing it if the Legislature passed one.

nj-united-states-senator-cory-booker.summary: Cory Booker is a Democrat who has represented New Jersey in the U.S. Senate since October 2013 and was previously mayor of Newark. Says the Iran war and Trump's tariffs have raised costs by $4,000 to $5,000 for the average New Jersey family, including higher fuel costs for small businesses and higher health care costs.
Proposes the Keep Your Pay Act, which would end federal income tax on the first $75,000 of income for most households and expand tax credits for working families.
Supports local policies that limit cooperation with ICE so that people come forward to report crimes regardless of immigration status. Says ICE sweeps have made immigrants afraid to contact police.
Introduced the Presidential Pardon Integrity Act, which he says would stop the pardon power from being used to reward political allies and campaign donors.

Says he secured $88.1 million for Cannon Air Force Base last year. Pledges to keep Cannon as an Air Force Special Operations base and to increase investment there.
Is sponsoring federal legislation to give more support to families caring for loved ones at home.
Says he grew up in and still lives in rural Nambé. Pledges investment in all 33 counties, including health care close to home, schools and infrastructure.
Says he was among the first Democrats to support efforts to block weapons sales to the Netanyahu government.

She faces Republican Gregg Hull in the November 3, 2026 general election, and her running mate for lieutenant governor is Stephanie Garcia Richard.

positions.stance: Pledges to expand existing tax breaks for lower-income families. Opposes Republican Gregg Hull's plan to gradually phase out New Mexico's personal income tax.
Proposes a state Office of Small Business and faster permitting. Supports raising the minimum wage to a living wage and growing industries such as technology, film, aerospace and outdoor recreation.
Says she would work toward a public health care option, protect and expand Medicaid, ban medical debt from credit reports, and address provider shortages with rural residency programs and incentives.
Supports a state commitment to net-zero emissions by 2050 and more renewable energy, community solar and battery storage. Proposes requiring data centers to supply their own energy infrastructure.
Says data centers should have guardrails and communities should take part in siting decisions. Opposes industries using about one million gallons of water per day.
Proposes limiting state and local cooperation with ICE, requiring agents to identify themselves and not wear masks, and barring ICE operations near schools, courthouses and health facilities.
Supports new requirements for firearms dealers, safe-storage measures and gun-violence prevention offices. Says she will work to get illegal guns off New Mexico streets.
Supports abortion access and reproductive rights, and has pledged to defend them as governor.
Proposes earlier detection of reading problems, universal child care, bilingual instruction, statewide community schools, career pathways and more dual-credit opportunities.
Proposes closing dark-money loopholes and strengthening lobbyist disclosure requirements.

Supports a bipartisan commission to identify ways to reduce the deficit. Says large corporations and the wealthy should pay their 'fair share.'

Supports continued U.S. security assistance to Israel, Ukraine and Taiwan. Introduced legislation to speed delivery of resources to Taiwan.

nh-united-states-senator-john-e-sununu.name: John E. Sununu
nh-united-states-senator-john-e-sununu.summary: John E. Sununu is a Republican from Hampton, New Hampshire. He represented the state in the U.S. House from 1997 to 2003 and in the U.S. Senate from 2003 to 2009, then spent close to two decades in the private sector. He won the Republican Senate primary on September 8, 2026, beating a field that included former Sen. Scott Brown, and faces Democrat Chris Pappas and Constitution Party candidate Edmond J. Laplante, Jr. in the general election.

positions.stance: Opposes abolishing ICE. Says ICE agents need better training, should not wear masks, and should all wear body cameras.
Supports congressional term limits as part of what he calls real reform in Congress.
Opposes granting citizenship to children born to people who travel to the U.S. to give birth. Says Congress should restrict this if the Supreme Court does not.
Supports tariffs aimed at China's trade practices but says tariffs should be set at reasonable rates with clarity and certainty, and that Congress has a big role to play.
Supports the 2025 tax and spending law (the One Big Beautiful Bill), citing its tax cuts on overtime, tips and Social Security, and its Medicaid work requirements.

Proposes letting insurers compete across state lines, requiring providers to post their prices, making health savings accounts available to anyone, and cutting federal regulation. Opposes Medicare for All.
Says the Social Security privatization plan he backed 20 years ago would have made the system solvent, and that today it should be fixed on a bipartisan basis.
Supports more domestic oil and gas production, permitting reform, and new pipelines and electric transmission lines to bring down energy costs in New Hampshire.
Supports requiring photo ID to vote and wants a straight up-or-down Senate vote on the voter ID provision.
Calls China the biggest national security threat. Supports continued military support for Taiwan and moving supply chains away from China.

Proposes ending U.S. funding for what he calls genocide abroad and moving those resources to housing, health care, and education.

Supports affordable, reliable, and resilient energy from a diverse portfolio. Favors grid modernization and market competition rather than government favoring particular industries, while respecting property rights and environmental stewardship.

Supports a strong national defense and honoring alliances. Says Congress must oversee military and intelligence activity, and the U.S. should avoid military engagements that lack clear objectives and constitutional authorization.

In an October 2026 podcast interview, discussed ranked choice voting and North Carolina's 2% ballot-access threshold for third parties as issues that affect voters' choices.
Supports strong judicial oversight, targeted investigations based on probable cause, and reforms that protect constitutional rights. Says government should collect only the data it needs.
Supports addiction treatment, proportional sentencing, due process, and focusing law enforcement on violent crime and organized trafficking.
Describes his approach to education as "liberty-first": protecting individual rights and limiting centralized power. His website says he supports inclusive sex education.

pa-governor-and-lieutenant-governor-stac.summary: Stacy Garrity, 62, of Bradford County, is Pennsylvania's state treasurer, first elected in 2020 and now serving her second term. Supports tax-break programs for companies as long as they support the community and a wide range of industries. Has announced plans to cut taxes and regulations in the Portland area.
In the Medford debate, said she would push for a moratorium on new data centers, as Gov. Kotek also did.

Supports SNAP food assistance and says her family relied on food stamps when she was a child. Criticizes the state's error rate in approving benefits and says the state should communicate better so recipients can stay eligible.

Says the state's current approach to struggling schools, with small step-by-step commitments to change, has not worked. Joined parents calling on Portland and Salem-Keizer district leaders to protect neighborhood schools.
Has spoken against needle exchanges near schools in Multnomah County.

Says she would govern independently of national politics, which she says has its own weather system she has never been dragged into. Argues a governor and a legislature from different parties can work together.
Has called for Portland City Councilor Mitch Green to resign over his comments about eliminating police, and criticizes Gov. Kotek for staying silent on them.

ri-governor-ken-block.name: Ken Block
ri-governor-ken-block.occupation: Software engineer and business owner. His firm works with governments and businesses to cut unnecessary spending.
ri-governor-ken-block.summary: Ken Block, 61, of Barrington, is a software engineer and government watchdog who announced an independent run for Rhode Island governor on April 2, 2026. This is his third run for governor: he ran in 2010 as the nominee of the Moderate Party, which he founded, and in 2014 as a Republican. He is on the November 3, 2026 general election ballot with Democrat Helena Buonanno Foulkes and Republican Aaron Guckian.

positions.stance: Says he would veto a millionaires tax if the legislature passed one. Says his aim is to cut expenses, not add taxes, and that a $15 billion budget should be enough.
Proposes cutting government-imposed charges on home and business electric bills. Would move necessary taxes off electric bills to what he calls fairer, more transparent ways of raising revenue.
Would suspend the state's truck-toll program and says he would veto any move to toll passenger vehicles.

Supports reviewing state-owned land and buildings for affordable housing and requiring a 'Housing Note' on bills showing their impact on housing. In the final debate he gave a range of 10,000 to 30,000 new homes and stressed simpler permitting.
Supports simpler permitting and regulation for developers, with buy-in from cities and towns. Says solar projects are taking thousands of acres of land that could be used for housing.
Would restore cost-of-living increases for people who retired before 2012. Proposes paying for them with excess pension-fund investment earnings rather than state tax revenue.

Says the state budget has nearly doubled in ten years. Proposes reviewing the operations, systems and staffing of every state agency, and called the Republican nominee's plan to cut $1.5 billion a 'fantasy.'

Says judicial selection is still highly political and would make merit the priority in appointments. Would move magistrate appointments away from the General Assembly to the same process used for judges.
Has declined to release his 2025 tax returns. He says his small business's pass-through filings could help competitors, and that he has 'been plenty transparent.'
Said yes when asked in the final debate whether the state should reexamine its sports betting laws.

dc-mayor-of-the-district-of-columbia-jan.summary: Janeese Lewis George is a Democrat who has represented Ward 4 on the Council of the District of Columbia since January 2021 and describes herself as a democratic socialist. She announced her campaign for mayor on December 1, 2025, after Mayor Muriel Bowser said she would not seek a fourth term. She won the June 16, 2026 Democratic primary with about 53% of the vote, and runner-up Kenyan McDuffie conceded on June 18.

positions.stance: Proposes building 72,000 homes in five years, expanding rent stabilization, prioritizing affordable housing, reforming zoning laws and streamlining permitting.

Says her administration would not clear encampment residents without a stable path to permanent housing. Supports funding housing vouchers, including Permanent Supportive Housing and the Local Rent Supplement Program.
Opposes the federal law-enforcement surge and National Guard deployment in D.C. She calls them an attack on the District's autonomy and has pledged to fight them.

Proposes to scale back the Metropolitan Police Department's cooperation with federal immigration officials and the federal 'Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful' task force starting on her first day in office.
Opposes quickly legalizing autonomous vehicles such as Waymo in D.C. She says expected AI-related job losses put workers, including drivers, at risk.
Says she and her team are preparing to tackle the District's rat problem directly, so that residents have safe and clean streets.

dc-mayor-of-the-district-of-columbia-rob.name: Robert L. Gross
dc-mayor-of-the-district-of-columbia-rob.summary: Robert L. Gross is a lifelong Washingtonian and technology professional. He is the DC Statehood Green Party's nominee for Mayor of the District of Columbia. He was unopposed on the party's June 16, 2026 primary ballot and won with 420 votes (53.9%), with write-ins taking the rest.

positions.stance: Proposes a "District Housing Utilization and Family Stability Act" that would split housing vouchers into family vouchers, with priority for households with children, and individual vouchers for single residents, seniors and workers.

Proposes a "Green Housing Modernization Standard" for new housing and major renovations, tied to the District's climate and affordability goals. Pledges to reform permitting and construction timelines and protect legacy residents and small businesses from displacement.
Pledges to make public safety agencies more transparent, expand mental-health interventions, and rebuild the relationship between the community and law enforcement.

Campaigns on a "Human Life Standard" that would judge each policy by whether it measurably improves residents' daily lives. Proposes streamlining city services and permits and modernizing government technology.
Pledges to expand after-school programs, restore vocational pipelines, and widen access to early childhood programs, apprenticeships and youth jobs across all wards.
Supports clean, electrified public transportation, green infrastructure, energy-efficient buildings and expanding the urban tree canopy.

Calls for local jobs, ownership opportunities and infrastructure investment east of the Anacostia River to close the income gap there. Pledges support for small businesses and fair, transparent contracting.
